title: The Tower Scribe's Signal
markdown:
Dawn came hard and bright through Farah’s tower window, laying restless color on her parchment. Birds made a cheerful noise of it. The air smelled of pine. Farah, the signal tower scribe, stretched fingers that were usually ink-stained and, today, strangely still. Her duty was to record the sunrise patterns for the capital. Under the calm, something buzzed. A prickle she did not like.

A THUD came from the valley. Then another. Then a third, each one a brutal mark on the quiet. Not a cart. Wrong. Farah scrambled to the highest viewport. Where the Lower Ridge tower had stood, dark smoke clawed the sky. Her heart answered it. She ran to the signal lenses and tried to hail the next tower. Nothing. She adjusted the prisms. Still silence. This was not an accident. The invasion force was cutting the message chain. The capital, unaware, was walking into a trap. She stuffed crystals and her sturdiest quill into a satchel. She had to reach Tomas. The ferryman’s son knew the fastest routes and the hidden ones.

At the riverbank Tomas was polishing the ferry, whistling as if the day had promised him nothing but glare on water. “Hey, Farah! Bright day for it.”

She nearly fell down the bank. “Tomas. We have a problem. A huge one.” The words tumbled. Towers down. Cut. The capital did not know.

He dropped the cloth. The grin went. “Cut? All of them?” He looked toward the peaks. “That’s bad.” He did not hesitate. “Hop on. We do not have a second.”

The ferry crossed like a dart. On the far side the path climbed toward the next tower on its rocky outcrop. “We have to get the message through,” Tomas said, taking the slope in long strides, “or the whole valley falls.”

The next tower was silent and damaged. Its main focusing crystal lay shattered, glittering like fallen stars. Farah’s shoulders dropped. “It’s broken.”

Tomas knelt among the shards. “Too clean for a rockslide. Someone smashed it. But look.” A smaller crystal still sat intact at the base. “Not the main one. Maybe enough.”

The main crystal amplified and threw the signal. This one would be a whisper. “It will not reach the capital,” Farah said.

Tomas’s grin came back, thinner, with a spark in it. “Not alone. Remember the emergency beacon they said was only for practice? Different energy. Stronger, if the alignment is exact. If we aim this crystal and hook the beacon… it might give us the push.” He looked at her. “Can you align it that precisely?”

Farah thought of the capital’s streets, of people who did not know a trap was closing. “Yes,” she said, and made the word stay. “I can.”

The next hour was all hands. Tomas rigged the humming beacon to the base. Farah, with Tomas holding a steady light, moved the small crystal by fractions. The sun sank into orange and purple. Shouts rose from below. The invaders were closer.

A gust hit the tower. The crystal shifted. “No!” Tomas lunged and caught it. His knuckles went white. He winced and held on. “Got it. Align it, Farah. Now.”

“Your hand—”

“It’s fine. A little pressure. Do it.”

She saw only the path for the signal. She locked the crystal. “Now. Power it.”

The beacon’s hum grew. The crystal pulsed and threw a thin brilliant line toward the distant capital, cutting the twilight.

“They’ll see it,” Farah whispered. “They’ll know.”

Grim figures in dark tunics burst onto the outcrop. They saw the beacon and the two silhouettes. “There they are.”

“Go,” Tomas said, pushing Farah toward a crevice he knew. “I’ll distract them.” He seized a loose rock. “Hey. Over here, you clods.” The stone clattered on the far side. Dust, metal, shouts. The invaders went after the noise.

Farah hesitated. He was buying her the path. She took it: into the crevice, down a goat track, loyalty burning as hard as fear. She did not look back until the slope had her. Then she ran for the landing, lungs raw, needing to tell someone and needing Tomas to be alive.

Hours later he limped in with his hand bandaged. Close calls. No worse. The capital, warned by that uncommon beam, had moved troops to the valley pass. The trap had closed on the enemy instead.

At the next dawn they stood by the river. The valley held. The towers would be repaired. “You were incredible,” Tomas said, worn and a little awed. “That alignment. I have never seen anything like it.”

Farah’s smile was real. “And you were brave. Really brave.” Yesterday’s fear had become a quieter strength.

“Today,” Tomas said, eyes bright again, “is going to be amazing.”

Farah nodded, ready for whatever the repaired chain would ask of them next.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, adventure story readers
